news.originalContent:
The U.S. Navy expects extended deployments to remain standard for the next several years as American warships continue operations related to the Iran war.

The Navy is warning sailors to expect deployments lasting 10 to 11 months for at least the next couple of years — rather than the traditional seven-month rotations — as operations in the Middle East continue to strain the fleet — according to USNI News. The extended deployments follow record-breaking missions by American aircraft carriers supporting the war against Iran, with Navy leadership acknowledging that the service needs more ships to shorten rotations and maintain operational readiness.

Longer deployments began in 2023, when Dwight D. Eisenhower Carrier Strike Group deployed for nine months, combatting the Houthis in the Red Sea. When America entered war with Iran, reportedly at Israel’s urging, deployments began to extend past 11 months.

The United States Navy did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment.

A feature of a too small Navy in a too dangerous world… this was predictable decade plus ago and we need to fix this and return deployments to nominal 6 months.

“The decision to extend our ships longer is a decision above the Navy,” Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy, John Perryman, told USNI News. “The president has a different calculus than we do, and so [the Pentagon makes] the decisions that they have to make, and then we support those decisions.” (RELATED: USS Abraham Lincoln Returns Home After One Of Longest Deployments In Naval History)

Ships currently being deployed to the Middle East are being sent out with enough supplies to sustain extended deployments, USNI News reported.

“You can kind of expect at least a 10-month deployment, and so that’s just the nature of what the capacity of the Navy can do,” Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle told USNI News. “I need a bigger Navy, and if you want to shorten the length of time of deployments, then obviously the math would say I need more capacity.”

This announcement comes less than a month after the USS Abraham Lincoln returned to the U.S. following a grueling extended deployment.

news.originalContent:
As every American who struggles to pay their rent, mortgage, gas, diesel, groceries, utilities, and healthcare premiums likely agrees, this midterm election is not really about affordability. As Bill Kristol’s son-in-law, Matthew Continetti, argues in The Wall Street Journal on Friday, it is “more than a gut check on Donald Trump’s presidency”; it is really about “antisemitism.” Antisemitism — not the Iran War, not diesel prices, not fertilizer prices, not the Trump administration’s bungled tariffs, not the government corruption, not the Trump family self-enrichment schemes, not the Epstein Files cover-up. No, it is antisemitism, according to Continetti. “Affordability comes and goes,” he writes (does it, though?), but “Antisemitism is a permanent stain.”

Before arriving at this stirring conclusion, Continetti scrutinizes all the popular progressives in the Democratic Party and their anti-Israel rhetoric, predictably giving them an F on their report cards. As he makes the case that the midterms are a referendum on whether America will become Nazi Germany, he also, very briefly, turns his attention to the right. Specifically, Thomas Massie.

“Rising antisemitism isn’t only a problem for Democrats,” says Continetti, who has a sinecure at the neocon think tank, American Enterprise Institute. “No one who travels in Republican or conservative circles can have missed rising anti-Israel sentiment and anti-Jewish prejudice among young men. Republicans have been able to remove antisemitic figures such as Rep. Thomas Massie (R., Ky.) and block antisemitic candidates such as Dan Bilzerian, a social media personality who ran for a Florida House seat. Yet antisemitism persists online and on podcasts.” (RELATED: ‘Not What We Thought MAGA Was Supposed To Be’: America First Skeptics Blast Iran Strikes)

Massie has earned this smear because he opposed writing blank checks to foreign governments — Ukraine, Israel, Qatar, or otherwise; opposed foreign intervention and the Iran War; had the gumption to call out the pro-Israel oligarch (a dual U.S.-Israeli citizen, for what it’s worth) Miriam Adelson for helping to bankroll his opponent, Ed Gallrein; correctly identified the power AIPAC has over Republican members of Congress; and, unlike most Republicans, actually took principled stances on the First Amendment and government censorship. In other words, the Kentucky congressman is anathema to someone like Continetti. Smart. Fully independent. America First. And is not, as so many in Conservatism Inc. are, driven by in-group virtue signaling and tribalistic conformity, or the fear of ostracizing donors who fund their institutions. Opposes militarism and is right about foreign intervention. Was right about the Iran War early on in March while Continetti was regurgitating “finish the job” talking points.

The problem here is that the definition of antisemitism, a word used so often and so fecklessly, no longer means anything. Just as, in the early 2020s, liberals watered down the definition of “racism” and “racist” to mean any policy or person that they did not like or wanted cancelled — if you believed in funding, not defunding the police, that made you a white supremacist during the summer of 2020, even if you were black — Continetti and other pro-Israel, neoconservative pundits, from Mark Levin to virtually every Fox News contributor, have similarly turned “antisemitism” into a weapon that allows them to smear and dismiss critics who poke too many holes in their pro-Israel narratives. Continetti references definitions of antisemitism given by Zionist and Harvard professor, Ruth Wisse and Soviet dissident and former Israeli official, Natan Sharansky. However, no different than a race-obsessed BLM activist, Continetti settles on his preferred definition: “I know when I see it.” Sure, that might work fine for judging whether a movie is pornographic, but judging an ideological opponent? It seems arbitrary and ripe for abuse, which is so often the case and is the case with Massie. (RELATED: Mark Levin Exposes His Deep Historical Ignorance With ‘Isolationist! Isolationist! Isolationist!’ Whining)

Further, Continetti lumps Massie with Dan Bilzerian, a loathsome internet celebrity who unsuccessfully ran to unseat Republican Florida Rep. Randy Fine earlier this year.* Bilzerian has actually used neo-Nazi rhetoric and spread repugnant Holocaust denial conspiracies; Massie has not. Yet Continetti does not make this distinction — and perhaps on purpose. This is yet another way that neocons try to dismiss critics of Israel. Besides bending the definition of antisemitism to an absurd degree, they smear by duplicitous and illogical games of association. All antisemites and neo-Nazis — say, an online Groyper — criticize Israel. Massie criticizes Israel. Therefore, Massie is an antisemite. It is piss-poor logic, no different than: All serial killers eat food; everyone eats food; therefore, everyone is a serial killer.

Continetti mindlessly throws around the “antisemitism” label without realizing his role in reducing it to an absurdity. (Are these Orthodox rabbis, critical of Israel, antisemites?) If one day, heaven forbid, a real neo-Nazi, who intends to use state power to persecute Jewish Americans and other minorities, rises to power, warnings will fall on deaf ears. In reducing every critic of Israel to an antisemite or neo-Nazi, Continetti and other neoconservatives have helped pave the road for real despotism. Of course, that vile despot is not Thomas Massie.

*Comparing Massie to Bilzerian is like comparing Norman Podhoretz to his son, John: one is intelligent and has principles, however flawed or flawless; the other is simply a goon.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by Darren McCollester/Newsmakers)

The provost of Dartmouth College resigned Wednesday after a faculty committee found that he used artificial intelligence to meaningfully alter his writing, including a guest column that appeared in The Washington Post.

Santiago Schnell voluntarily resigned from his role as provost, Dartmouth College President Sian Leah Beilock confirmed in a statement, according to WCAX.

“I expect our senior leaders to hold themselves to the highest standards. Out of respect for his colleagues and the institution, Santiago has resigned as provost and is leaving the university. This was his decision. We remain grateful for his leadership and wish him well,” Beilock said.

Schnell’s decision to resign from his role as provost of the university follows the release of an Oct. 27 memorandum detailing the results of a faculty-led investigation into his writings.

Schnell “used AI to meaningfully alter his writing in violation of at least one publication’s AI use and/or disclosure requirement, failed to disclose his use of AI in clear violation of a national newspaper’s stated policy, was not forthcoming about his AI use, and fell short of the standards set forth by Dartmouth’s Code of Ethical Conduct, the Academic Honor Principle, and Geisel’s Policy on Expectations for Professionalism for Faculty, Non-Faculty Academics, and Staff,” according to the same memo.

An Aug. 9 column attributed to Schnell titled, “Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem,” that appeared in the Washington Post was determined to be 100 percent AI-written, according to Semafor.

Semafor scanned multiple guest columns featured in the opinion pages of the Washington Post, New York Times, and Wall Street Journal using the AI detector Pangram.

Schnell defended his column at the time.

“I wrote this essay based on my own thinking. Then, I used ChatGPT to refine a few arguments, check for grammatical errors, and submit it to the Washington Post,” Schnell told Semafor, adding that his column “went through multiple rounds of edits by the Post.” (RELATED: Tech Giant Floats Bill That Would Let Feds Step In Only When More Than 50 Lives Are On The Line)

Following Semafor’s Aug. 26 investigation, Dartmouth College’s newspaper, The Dartmouth, also reviewed Schnell’s writings from before and after November 2022, when ChatGPT was released to the public. The Dartmouth found Schnell’s works authored before 2022 were “100% human-written,” while nine of his works authored this year were likely “96% AI-written,” according to results from Pangram.

Schnell described himself as a “mathematical biologist” on his LinkedIn page. He taught mathematics, biomedical data science, and biochemistry and cell biology at Dartmouth College.

News of Schnell’s voluntary departure comes amid a three-day conference on AI being hosted at the college.

news.originalContent:
(Getty Images/Donato Fasano)

A Syrian hacker who targeted the U.S. Marine Corps and triggered a $136 billion Wall Street flash crash while working for former dictator Bashar al-Assad’s regime has been sentenced to federal prison.

Ahmad Umar Agha received a 42-month prison sentence for his role in a sweeping cyber conspiracy targeting approximately 47 Western organizations, including American government agencies and media outlets, according to a Thursday press release from the Department of Justice. The Assad-linked operation attempted to persuade American Marines to disobey orders, infiltrate White House social media accounts and spread disinformation that temporarily wiped over $100 billion from the value of stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average.

“Agha deployed his hacking skills in the service of Assad’s regime to silence reporting on the regime’s atrocities, intimidate its opponents, and incite U.S. servicemembers to refuse their orders”, said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg in the release. “His attacks on our networks and institutions, including one that temporarily erased $136 billion from U.S. investors, constitute an assault on the free press and our national and economic security. Today’s sentence should serve as a reminder of the National Security Division’s long memory in pursuit of state-sponsored hackers such as Agha.” (RELATED: Syrian President Bashar Al-Assad Flees To Russia After Losing Grip On Power)

The DOJ did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment.

Syrian Man Sentenced for Wide-Ranging Hacking Conspiracy Conducted on Behalf of the Bashar Al Assad Regime Ahmad Umar Agha (also known as Th3Pr0) had spent more than a decade as a fugitive for targeting of Western media entities, businesses, NGOs, and U.S. and allied government entities. “Agha deployed his hacking skills in the service of Assad’s regime to silence reporting on the regime’s atrocities, intimidate its opponents, and incite U.S. servicemembers to refuse their orders,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “His attacks on our networks and institutions, including one that temporarily erased $136 billion from U.S. investors, constitute an assault on the free press and our national and economic security. Today’s sentence should serve as a reminder of the National Security Division’s long memory in pursuit of state-sponsored hackers such as Agha.” 🔗: https://t.co/9Tiyg2IRiQ

Agha attempted on several occasions to gain access to the White House social media page, per the DOJ release. He hacked the Twitter account of the Associated Press, claiming that the then-president Obama was injured due to multiple explosions at the White House, leading to a $136 billion stock market drop.

He additionally gained access to the company hosting the Marine Corps recruitment website. He then redirected site visitors to a site encouraging Marines to refuse orders and fight for the Syrian Army, according to the statement.

“This case emphasizes the grave threat posed by cyber criminals and especially those serving regimes hostile to the United States,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Theophani K. Stamos for the Eastern District of Virginia said in the statement. “The protection of our electronic infrastructure, financial markets, and the companies that serve the American people is of paramount importance. We will pursue and prosecute anyone who endangers the systems that reinforce our national security or undermines the institutions on which our people rely.”

news.originalContent:

President Donald Trump on Saturday made a last-minute plea to New Yorkers to vote for Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman on Election Day, saying the Nassau County executive can save the Empire State from Gov. Kathy Hochul’s “failed and incompetent” leadership.

“Kathy Hochul may be the worst governor in the history of New York State and one of the worst in the nation,” roared the commander-in-chief during a tele-rally promoting the campaigns of Blakeman and two other New York Republicans, Attorney General candidate Saritha Komatireddy and upstate congressional hopeful Anthony Constantino.

“She been a disaster, and I can tell you that Bruce has been a friend of mine for a long time,” Trump added.

“Anybody that can do what he did in politics and get resounding results, and not only that, he has the safest county in the United States of America [according to US News & World Report] … He’s a great manager.”

Despite recent polls showing Hochul ahead anywhere from 11 to 14 points, Trump said he expects the Nassau County executive to win.

“I’ll be waiting for his call,” the president said. “I bet he’s going to be one of the first calls if he wins, and he’ll get tremendous help from the federal government. And it’s hard to help people that do such a bad job. It’s almost like throwing good money after bad.”

Hochul spokesperson Ryan Radulovack responded by attempting to paint Trump as a boogeyman, something the governor has also done many times throughout the campaign.

“Blakeman … started with the promise to ‘bring Trump-style leadership to Albany,’ and his closing message is telling people how little he regrets going full Trump in this campaign,” added Radulovack.

“Gov. Hochul has put money back in New Yorkers’ pockets, invested $4 billion in public safety, and fought back against Trump’s attacks,” while Blakeman “defends everything Trump does.”

Trump during the tele-rally also found some time to claim that the war with Iran is all but over.

“We’re winning very easily the war with Iran,” Trump said.

A major human trafficking operation in Placer County resulted in nearly two dozen men busted for alleged sex solicitation, drug possession and more.

Undercover agents with the Placer County Sheriff’s Office Operations Unit conducted a two-day sting where they contacted sex buyers throughout the county. The operation busted 21 men cited for soliciting prostitution, the sheriff’s office said.

During the sting, agents contacted individuals who were “attempting to purchase sex, sometimes referred to as ‘johns.'”

Four of the would-be sex buyers were also cited for drug possession, the sheriff’s office said.

Authorities said one of the men was found to be carrying a concealed, loaded firearm without a permit. He will face additional charges.

Video from the operation showed agents chasing after suspects and other clips of men being handcuffed.

“Human trafficking is complex, and there is no single approach to addressing it,” the sheriff’s office said.

“In Placer County, law enforcement and our community partners work from several different angles, including identifying and supporting survivors, investigating traffickers and addressing the factors that can contribute to exploitation.”

Representatives with Stand Up Placer, a nonprofit organization that helps survivors of sexual assault and human trafficking, and agents spoke with cited individuals “about the impact their actions can have and the connection between the purchase of sex and human trafficking,” according to the sheriff’s office.

Markle Sr., 82, was seen being moved between care facilities in Lakeland, Florida, on Saturday, in photos obtained by Page Six. The former Hollywood lighting director was being pushed in a wheelchair by aides.

Markle Sr. left his home in Cebu in May for Florida following a stroke that led to a blood clot, and the subsequent amputation of his left leg.

News broke last week that Thomas Jr. had allegedly found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in four large boxes at his dad’s home.

Thomas Jr., 60, told the Sun he was looking for a phone belonging to Thomas Sr.’s much-younger Filipino girlfriend when he stumbled upon the alleged photos “mixed up with innocent family mementos.”

Thomas Jr. said he was “horrified” by the “huge piles of evidence” and felt he had “no option but to report” his father.

news.originalContent:
In a counterprotest, Netanyahu supporters demand that Israel should not have a government with ‘terrorists’.

Thousands of people have rallied in Tel Aviv to urge the Israeli opposition to make a deal with Arab parties to remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Protesters at Saturday’s rally told the AFP news agency this may be the “last chance for real change” and that Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is a “great manipulator”.

Main opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has previously ruled out forming a coalition with Israel’s Arab parties, but a deadlock in Tuesday’s elections means siding with the parties could help him form a government.

“People really want this vote for change to work out, and they believe that… Gadi Eisenkot and other leaders of the Jewish-Israeli parties need to listen to their voice,” Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh said from Ramallah on Saturday.

Counter-protesters also showed up to Saturday’s demonstrations, with Netanyahu supporters seen shouting their own demands that “Israel should not have a government with so-called terrorists”, Odeh said.

Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s elections, while Eisenkot’s won 48, meaning neither side can form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament alone.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

There’s a theory in the bourbon world that women are better at tasting the spirit than men, and some experts say there’s scientific proof to back up the claim.

Smelling is an important step in the tasting process, and there is some evidence that suggests women have an advantage in that area.

“Women have a keener sense of smell and taste than men,” Louisville, Kentucky-based whiskey expert and author Susan Reigler told Fox News Digital.

Reigler, who is also a former president of the Bourbon Women organization, cited a scientific paper published in 2014 that explored the differences in the olfactory bulbs of men and women

The report showed that women have just under 50% more neurons than men in olfactory regions, a difference that could contribute to a stronger sense of smell.

“There are a number of different factors that come to play and certainly things that are outside of smell that affect men and women differently,” Caitlin McLean, the vice president of Qualitative Solutions at MMR Research Worldwide’s North American offices in New York, told Fox News Digital.

McLean noted that there’s more to tasting bourbon than just what happens in the mouth and on the palate.

The processes of orthonasal and retronasal olfaction play big roles in the tasting experience.

Orthonasal olfaction occurs when aromas enter through the nostrils, such as smelling aromas, while retronasal olfaction occurs when those aromas “are coming up in sort of the back of your palate and hitting the nose from the inside,” McLean explained.

“When we think about what’s critical to bourbon, some of those distinctive notes, like vanilla and cinnamon and leather and tobacco, smoke, dark fruit, all of those are identified through retronasal olfaction,” she said.

Retronasal olfaction is incredibly important when tasting bourbon because the flavors that arise at the end of the drinking process define the complexity, finish and overall enjoyment of the beverage, McLean said, adding that “the tongue and the palate can only taste so much.”

Hormones also come into play, too, McLean noted, especially estrogen, which is associated with a heightened sense of smell.

“So in moments of pregnancy or menopause, you do see strong differentiation in olfactory sensitivity,” McLean said.

The belief that women are better bourbon tasters is partially rooted in the idea that women are biologically wired to have a stronger sense of smell and taste as a way to protect their children, a theory that is difficult to prove with data.

“There is some scientific evidence that women, on average, outperform men in olfactory tasks, but maternal instinct is a difficult one to prove scientifically,” McLean said.

Whether or not they’re scientifically proven to be better at tasting the spirit, women have been known to hold their own on the Kentucky Bourbon Trail, according to Reigler.

“Historically, the bourbon distillers in Kentucky, their tasting panels, their quality control panels, were always majority of women,” she said.

Men can still be excellent tasters, too, Reigler noted. Ultimately, she said, for anyone to become a truly skilled taster, “it just takes practice.”

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Archaeologists have identified Europe’s largest known collection of Iron Age iron bars in Austria — raising the possibility that the valuable cargo was lost in a shipwreck on the Danube River more than 2,000 years ago.

Workers recovered at least 500 bars, making the collection the largest known Iron Age find of its kind in Europe. The “rusty treasure,” as researchers called it in a press release, would have been extremely valuable during the Iron Age, when iron production and trade were expanding across Europe.

“Fortunately, the gravel workers [who found the iron bars] reported this find to the Monuments Authority and did not sell them to a scrap dealer,” Peter Trebsche, a professor at the University of Innsbruck in Austria, told Fox News Digital.

The iron bars — which weigh more than a metric ton in total — could have been used to forge roughly 500 swords weighing between 3.3 and 4.4 pounds each, according to the researchers.

The research was published earlier this fall by archaeologist Trebsche as well as archaeologist Marion Berranger in the journal Antiquity.

The iron bars were originally discovered in 2019 during gravel extraction work in Deinham, Austria.

Researchers used radiocarbon dating to determine the age of the iron bars, which likely date to the third or second century B.C.

While its intended destination remains unknown, researchers believe the iron may have been forged in Bavaria, Germany, before being transported along the Danube River.

The discovery sheds new light on the scale of ancient iron production, which has been difficult to measure because iron objects are often overlooked or difficult to date the researchers said.

“Fortunately, the gravel workers reported this find to the Monuments Authority and did not sell them to a scrap dealer.”

“Therefore, the discovery of numerous double-pointed iron objects during gravel extraction along the River Danube provided a unique opportunity to investigate large-scale prehistoric iron production and trade,” the press release said.

In a statement, Trebsche called the discovery “nothing short of a minor miracle.”

He added, “I am sincerely grateful to the finders that [the workers] decided to donate this extraordinary trove to a state museum collection.”

Trebsche told Fox News Digital the iron bars were found during gravel extraction work in an old, silt-filled channel of the Danube River.

He said a shipwreck is the most plausible explanation for how the bars ended up in the river, although no remains of a vessel were found.

“No parts of the ship were recovered, because this section of the Danube poses some dangers to navigation like stone balls and sand banks,” Trebsche noted.

“In support of this interpretation is also the fact that none of the finds shows signs of intentional destruction, which would be indicative of a ritual offering during the Late Iron Age.”

He also said the 500-sword figure is only an estimate, as the iron could have been used to make tools or jewelry instead of weapons.

“The amount of iron from Deinham is about ten times larger than the largest iron hoard finds of that period,” he said.

Trebsche said the most surprising aspect of the discovery was the sheer quantity of iron being transported at once — and the fact that so much was available for a single trade transaction during the Late Iron Age.

“This finding demonstrates the increased capacities of iron production that were reached in the 3rd/2nd century BC in the Danube region,” he said.

A number of other Iron Age discoveries have been announced across Europe over the past year.

Earlier this year, archaeologists uncovered a 2,000-year-old temple in Denmark at a major Iron Age settlement that once served as a regional center of power and wealth.

At around the same time, researchers announced the discovery of rare four-wheeled wagon remains among 950 Iron Age metal objects unearthed in northern England, marking the first potential evidence of such vehicles in Britain.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

This year’s NYC Marathon carries a lot of personal weight for Joe Macklin — who’s running after losing a jaw-dropping 190 pounds.

The 432-pound Staten Islander realized he needed to make a change to his own life after he learned that an acquaintance had lost theirs.

“In September of 2024, a friend of a friend, who was very heavy, ended up passing away,” Macklin, 25, who now weighs 240 pounds, told The Post on Friday from the pickleball court at St. Christopher in Dongan Hills.

So he decided to get gastric bypass surgery.

“And I was like, ‘You know what? I’m healthy enough, let’s see what the doctor says if I’m able to get the surgery,’ because we always talked about it.”

Even before he went under the knife, he started shedding weight.

The requirements for the five-hour surgery was that he follow a liquid diet, undergo an endoscopy, see a cardiologist and get evaluated by a psychologist.

Right after his successful surgery at Staten Island University Hospital in December 2024, he was already down to 388 pounds.

In a week he dropped an additional 20 pounds — and it was off to the races from there.

“After that, once I started exercising, I was losing 10 to 12 pounds a week,” he said.

Three months after surgery, he started to think about running the TCS New York City Marathon.

“I always kept saying, ‘I want to run the marathon,’ and I was like, ‘With that weight I’ll never run,'” said Macklin, who grew up in Emerson Hill and still lives there.

He started by walking with his mother, Renee.

“I would walk for 45 minutes alone, and then I would bring her for 25 minutes. So then those walks ended up becoming me starting to run,” he said.

As fate would have it, Macklin’s father, John, is a director of operations at Brean Capital and the boss of former Bengals and Jets quarterback Boomer Esiason’s nephew. And in July, received a call that the athlete’s foundation needed an additional runner for the Nov. 1 marathon.

“He said, ‘I have a spot open … We’re desperately looking for somebody. Would Joe be interested? You have two minutes to answer,'” Macklin recalled.

He had a week to officially confirm his spot, so he got his health checked, having suffered an ulcer the previous November.

“I had like till 4 p.m. that day to declare and it was my girlfriend’s best friend’s wedding. And I had an endoscopy and I told the doctor, ‘Doc, I gotta be out of here in a half hour, my girlfriend’s gonna kill me,'” he said.

“I got changed in the endoscopy room just to get there.”

The Boomer Esiason Foundation gave him a 16-week training program to follow ahead of the 26.2-mile race through the five boroughs, which Macklin then adapted to fit his routine.

“I just followed my gut, like what’s been working for me, and then I built the tolerance of like seven miles to 10 miles. And where I live is all up and downhill, so three miles was really like four miles,” he said.

Macklin, a Manhattan HVAC mechanic, runs every day after work from 5 to 6 p.m. and then plays pickleball from 7 to 9 p.m.

In September, he ran the Staten Island Half Marathon, clocking in at two hours and 26 minutes and beating his goal by four minutes.

“That’s what really made me feel confident about the marathon,” he said.

The now avid runner, who still sticks to his post-surgery diet of “a lot of protein and some carbs,” like steak, grilled chicken and rice, said his goal is to run the marathon in five hours.

On race day, his parents, aunts, uncles and cousins will be there cheering him on, as well as his girlfriend, Gwyn, whom he met while they were students at St. John’s University.

His father’s birthday happens to fall on the day of the marathon, so afterwards, Macklin, an Edmonton Oilers fan, will watch them take on the Rangers at The Kettle Black, a sports bar on Staten Island, with his family and Gwyn.

With the Boomer Esiason Foundation, Macklin’s running in support of cystic fibrosis, and so far, he’s raised over $6,300 — and said his pickleball teammates really stepped up their donation game.

“There’s a lot of older women that I play with, and I just tap the ball because I don’t want to hurt anybody, and those people are the ones who gave donations,” he said.

“So my generosity paid off.”

A dispute over the politicisation of Poland’s constitutional court is deepening, with no side appearing to back down.

The Polish president has held crisis talks with political leaders as a dispute over the independence of the country’s top constitutional court deepens.

Representatives of nationalist, far-right, and some governing coalition parties attended President Karol Nawrocki’s talks at the presidential palace on Saturday, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s governing centrist party, Civic Coalition, stayed away.

Nawrocki said in a statement that he convened the “urgent” consultations “due to the threat to Poland’s internal security” presented by the sudden suspension on Friday of the Constitutional Tribunal’s chief judge, Bogdan Swieczkowski.

No breakthrough had emerged by Saturday afternoon.

Meanwhile, in a Saturday evening speech addressing the ongoing crisis, Tusk accused conservative nationalist opposition leaders of wanting to “destroy democracy and rule of law”.

“Let’s call things by their name,” he said. “For years in Poland there exist organisations and politicians who wish to destroy democracy and rule of law.”

news.originalContent:
Refugee and migrant boats are rarely found in Dutch waters, and authorities are still trying to establish where this one came from.

Authorities in the Netherlands have rescued 38 people found adrift in a rubber boat off the Dutch coast, in one of the first such interceptions for the country.

Two of the people on board the dinghy when it was rescued are thought to be smugglers, while the rest are migrants, military police spokesperson Doron Wallin told The Associated Press news agency on Saturday.

“We don’t know where they came from – France, the Netherlands or Belgium – and we don’t know where the boat was heading,” Wallin said.

The boat was discovered drifting with no motor off the coast of the Netherlands’ Zeeland province, far southwest of Amsterdam. No one was wearing a life vest.

All 38 on the boat were men, 36 of whom were from Afghanistan, and two – the suspected smugglers – were from Sudan, according to the AFP news agency. The two Sudanese men have been arrested on suspicion of people smuggling.

It is not known where the boat was headed, but refugee and migrant crossings in small boats from France to the United Kingdom have become commonplace in recent years. It is unusual for boats to be discovered in Dutch waters, however.

“These are things you usually see in France and Belgium. We rarely see it here in the Netherlands before today,” Wallin said.

Dutch authorities will open an investigation into the case on Sunday.

news.originalContent:
Judge permanently drops Trump’s $10bn WSJ lawsuit, ruling the president failed to prove actual malice in the newspaper’s reporting.

A federal judge has permanently dismissed United States President Donald Trump’s multibillion-dollar defamation lawsuit against media mogul Rupert Murdoch and The Wall Street Journal.

On Saturday, US District Judge Darrin Gayles concluded that the president had failed to establish the standard of “actual malice” required for defamation suits.

Under US law, a successful complaint must show that the defendant released a defamatory statement knowing it was false or with “reckless disregard” for its accuracy.

Gayles, however, said that Trump was “grasping at straws” with his $10bn case against The Wall Street Journal.

“The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice,” Gayles wrote.

“Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.”

The judge went so far as to suggest that Trump’s legal team had attempted “to manufacture flaws with the investigation” published in The Wall Street Journal.

The case stemmed from coverage that linked Trump to the late disgraced financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

On July 17, 2025, The Wall Street Journal published an exclusive describing a sexually suggestive birthday note gifted to Epstein for his 50th birthday in 2003, as part of a book of congratulatory letters.

The letters were reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell, who is serving a 20-year prison sentence for her involvement in Epstein’s sex-trafficking scheme.

The note attributed to Trump includes typed text framed by a hand-drawn outline of what appears to be a curvaceous woman. At the bottom, where her pelvic region might be, is Trump’s signature.

Trump vehemently denied responsibility for the text, the signature and the artwork. A copy of the birthday letter was later released through the House Oversight Committee.

The Wall Street Journal’s article came at a time when Trump’s second administration was facing intense scrutiny over whether it had withheld documents about Epstein’s alleged sex crimes, despite promises of transparency.

Critics had also raised questions about the nature of Trump and Epstein’s relationship. The two men appear to have socialised together, and Epstein was known to have surrounded himself with powerful figures from politics, academia and the business world.

In 2025, Trump said he ended his relationship with Epstein after the financier “stole” female employees from his Mar-a-Lago resort.

Epstein was convicted of soliciting a minor for sex in Florida in 2008, for which he served 13 months in jail. In 2019, he faced federal charges related to sex trafficking, but he was found dead in his New York City jail cell before he could be brought to trial. His death was later ruled a suicide.

Legal advocates say Epstein’s victims are estimated to number in the hundreds.

After the release of The Wall Street Journal report, Trump branded the newspaper’s coverage “false, malicious, and defamatory”.

His lawsuit, filed in the federal court in Miami on July 18, 2025, accused the paper and its reporters of having “knowingly and recklessly” published “numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements”.

The result, it alleged, was “overwhelming financial and reputational harm” to the president. Two journalists associated with The Wall Street Journal article were named among the defendants.

In April, Judge Gayles dismissed the defamation lawsuit, ruling that Trump had failed to prove the reporting was borne of “actual malice”.

But that initial ruling gave Trump the opportunity to refile his complaint, which he did in May.

The updated lawsuit claimed The Wall Street Journal had been reckless in not showing how reporters had received and verified the letter.

Saturday’s Miami ruling deals a final blow to Trump’s attempt to sue over the issue. Gayles’s decision dismisses the case “with prejudice”, which effectively blocks any future litigation on the matter.

Trump has other ongoing defamation cases against other media outlets, including the BBC and The New York Times.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Now he wants to take a crack at the bench.

A Staten Island civil judge candidate has a wild, action-packed past as an undercover narc who posed as a dope fiend to bust dealers in NYC back in the 1980s.

Glenn Yost told The Post he made more than 500 drug busts with the NYPD – including the very first grand jury crack-sale case on Staten Island.

“I feel like I’ve come full circle in the law – enforcing it for 20 years, teaching it, and practicing it for nearly 20 years,” said the 63-year-old Republican lawyer.

Yost was born in Brooklyn and moved to Staten Island when he was 11 years old. He was raised by a single mother who worked at Sears.

He was 20 years old when he joined the NYPD and became part of the narcotics unit two years into his career, he said.

He ran undercover operations for the NYPD in Brooklyn, Manhattan and Staten Island under an alias. Deep undercover, he lived in a wiretapped apartment in Brooklyn and had fake ID and credit cards.

He assumed new identities like “Vinnie” – a red Eldorado Cadillac-driving aspiring actor who summered in the Hamptons, but hung out in squalor-filled crack houses to score heroin, cocaine and prescription pain med Percocet.

“Those shooting galleries, if there’s anything you can imagine close to hell, that would be it,” he said.

“It was scary because you didn’t know, you didn’t know who was who. You didn’t know if you were going to get robbed. It smelled horrible. People would go to the bathroom wherever they wanted to.”

Consistency helped him gain the dealers’ trust — so he became a repeat customer. A confidential informant helped cement the relationships.

“I think ideally what the undercover needs to be is very clever and cunning,” Yost said.

Sometimes, he was forced at gunpoint to sample the drugs to prove he wasn’t a cop. But Yost  mastered the art of pretending to sample the goods by dipping his forefinger in the powder — but bringing his middle finger to his mouth. Dealers, he said, “never noticed.”

If he was asked to shoot up heroin on the spot, “I just pushed them away and started yelling and screaming.”

And just in case, he kept a .25 automatic Colt pistol hidden under his clothes for protection.

Yost played the part so well that one of the criminals he took down, “JD [John Doe] Handsome,” developed a deep friendship with his alter-ego.

“I kind of liked him,” Yost admitted. “He was a good person – other than being a drug dealer … He was thinking of making me the godfather of his kid.”

He first crossed paths with JD Handsome during a botched cocaine buy, when another dealer snatched his $20 and bolted. Handsome saw an opportunity, sidling over to ask how he could help.

Over the operation’s six months, the two were practically inseparable, hanging out to all hours of the night.

When he finally arrested his ‘pal’ and his pregnant, coke-dealing wife, the couple were stunned.

“If you can imagine the shock on this guy. I mean, I’m his friend,” Yost said. “He was just in complete shock [when they were arrested]. He could not get over the fact that I was a police officer.”

The key to selling his junkie bit was never taking no for an answer, Yost said.

“A heroin addict wants the heroin. If they tell you know ‘no,’ you still hang around and beg until you get what you want,” he said.

Yost went on to work as a youth outreach officer, co-founding the “No Staten Island Racism” school program before attending New York Law School and retiring from the NYPD at 40.

While studying for the bar, he taught criminal justice and history at St. John’s University and St. Joseph by the Sea high school on Staten Island.

He believes his unique background helped him empathize with all walks of life.

“I bring life experience, compassion, patience, and respect to the bench,” said the married father of five. “Compassion comes from observing and being part of people’s suffering.”

“Nobody Wants This” star Tovah Feldshuh swears there is no squabbling amongst the cast over the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

“Tensions are NOT RISING. Profound differences of opinion are,” Feldshuh, 77, wrote via Threads on Friday, October 30, addressing rumors the cast is feuding. “Please do not conflate the two — And none of it will be brought to the set.”

She continued, “I deeply enjoy filming NWT and hope we are chosen to go on for a fourth season.”

Last month, Adam Brody, who plays a rabbi in the Netflix series, spoke up about the Middle East strife.

“I have spoken a lot about it privately. I haven’t spoken much about it publicly,” the “O.C.” alum shared in GQ. “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine.

“It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago. I’m hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.”

Feldshuh, who plays Brody’s mother, Bina, in the series, vehemently disagrees with her on-screen son.

“To accuse the Jewish people of genocide is wild,” she told The Post. “It’s right out of Hitler’s playbook. You take the victim and you make the victim the perpetrator.”

“My job, as Bina but also as Tovah, is to love the people on set at my place of work, to be kind,” she said.

Rabbi Steve Leder, who was the technical adviser on the show’s first season, has also blasted Brody, labeling him an “ignorant Jew.”

The series follows Rabbi Noah Roklov (Brody), who is in a relationship with Joanne, a non-Jewish sex podcaster, played by Kristen Bell.

It is loosely based on creator Erin Foster’s relationship with now-husband Simon Tikhman.

Season 3 of the rom-com series recently dropped.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

There’s a UCLA coach who has sparked a major transformation in addition to Bob Chesney.

How about that Colin Hitschler defense?

For more than a month now, Hitschler’s unit has been in lockdown mode.

The Bruins haven’t given up more than two touchdowns in a game since the middle of September, and on Saturday they unveiled a masterpiece at the Rose Bowl.

With its offense sputtering for much of the afternoon, No. 7 UCLA’s defense stepped up in a major way during a 27-0 victory over Nevada.

The Bruins (8-0) intercepted four passes — with a drop by safety Scooter Jackson preventing a fifth — while holding the Wolf Pack (3-5) to 176 yards of offense.

It was UCLA’s first shutout since a 2015 thrashing of Oregon State and its first at home since holding Oregon scoreless in 2007.

These guys don’t call themselves the Bruin Bullies for nothing.

The Bruins’ defense is one of the biggest reasons they remain in College Football Playoff contention and have won on days when their offense has been sluggish.

Over its last five games, UCLA has given up an average of only seven points. That’s a number they often gave up in less than a quarter under the likes of Jerry Azzinaro, Tom Bradley and some of the other defensive coordinators who preceded Hitschler.

Nevada’s best chance to put points on the board came late in the third quarter, when it missed a 48-yard field goal.

The game ended in fitting fashion, with defensive back Ty Lee making an interception in the final minute and the Bruins taking a knee to run out the clock.

The Bruins kept their unbeaten start rolling ahead of the initial release of the CFP rankings on Tuesday.

The big question is if they will be one of the top eight teams, which would put them in position to host a first-round game at the Rose Bowl.

With one of the quarterfinal games also scheduled to be played at the Rose Bowl, it’s conceivable that UCLA could play back-to-back home games in the CFP.

With UCLA’s offense generating very little, Bruins defensive back Derrick Barksdale took it upon himself to put points on the board.

Barksdale intercepted a pass midway through the first quarter and returned it 26 yards for a touchdown, putting his team up 10-0.

After four drives that basically went nowhere, UCLA’s offense finally showed up on a 71-yard drive that ended when quarterback Ty Dieffenbach faked a handoff and plunged into the end zone for a 4-yard touchdown. The Bruins were up 17-0, and that was essentially the ballgame.

UCLA edge rusher Sahir West made 1 ½ sacks and two tackles for loss, including one for an 8-yard loss on third down early in the fourth quarter that forced the Wolf Pack to punt from their end zone.

West finished the game with nine tackles, continually pressuring Nevada’s quarterbacks.

The Bruins had a special welcome for former teammate Luke Duncan in his return to the Rose Bowl. Jackson intercepted Duncan’s first pass, returning it to the Nevada 28-yard line and setting up a UCLA field goal for the game’s opening points.

Nevada’s second drive ended with another interception, this one by UCLA linebacker Jalen Woods.

The Wolf Pack yanked Duncan in favor of A.J. Bianco after his third interception, though Duncan returned in the second half.

The Bruins face one of their toughest remaining tests next weekend when they travel to face Minnesota. The Golden Gophers are particularly tough at Huntington Bank Stadium, where they’ve beaten Michigan and Iowa.

On the heels of this year’s horror hit “Obsession,” breakout star Inde Navarrette make her “Saturday Night Live” hosting debut tonight.

It’s only the fifth time in the show’s 52-season history that an episode has aired live on Halloween night; the most recent was a 2020 Halloween show hosted by John Mulaney (who will become a seven-timer in November).

It’s a fitting night for one of the horror genre’s newest scream queens to host the sketch series.

Navarrette will be joined by musical guest Gracie Abrams, who just announced the deluxe version of her latest album “Daughter from Hell.” Abrams made her “SNL” debut in December 2024.

Yes! “SNL” is on live tonight, Oct. 31.

Tonight’s Halloween episode of “SNL” will air live coast-to-coast at 11:30 p.m. ET/8:30 p.m. PT, though it may be subject to delays due to college football in certain time zones.

If you don’t have cable, you’ll need a live TV streaming service to stream Inde Navarrette on “SNL” for free.

DIRECTV is our favorite service for trying live TV for free. Right now, you can take advantage of a five-day free trial before saving $30 on your first month. We recommend the Choice plan, which includes NBC as part of its 125+ channel options.

You can also watch “SNL” for free with a Peacock Premium free trial (seven days, then $16.99/month). Peacock also has new “SNL” episodes available to stream in full on Sunday mornings.

Actress Inde Navarrette will host “SNL” for the first time tonight, Oct. 31.

“Saturday Night Live” is back from a two week break in time for Halloween. Below, find the confirmed episode dates for the rest of Season 52, through the end of 2026.

After the cast grew by five last season, the Season 52 cast only features two new hires. Here’s who you can expect to see in sketches tonight and throughout the season.

Giants running back Cam Skattebo was handed a fine for a use-of-helmet violation — a flag he was already pretty upset about.

Get texts from Paul Schwartz with all the latest Giants news and insights, exclusive to Sports+ subscribers.

The NFL fined Skattebo $7,073 for his illegal use of the helmet during the Giants’ 27-21 win over the Texans on Sunday.

Out of the eight people fined for use-of-helmet infractions across the league in Week 7, Skattebo was the only one who was given a flag in real time, a move that the running back blasted the officials for.

Skattebo, 24, did not hold back when talking to reporters about the flag following Sunday’s win.

“But I will say, man, the NFL loves to post [about] me when I do stuff like that — but then also wants to take stuff from me,” he said, according to NJ.com. “I’m going to run the ball like I want to run the ball. And if I’m going to continue to get flagged for it or fined for it, man, I guess I’m going to play for free.

“I’m going to do what I can to be on this team, to give everything I’ve got. And if they’re going to punish me for that, then I’m just going to keep doing it and keep playing hard.”

Giants right guard Francis Mauigoa concurred that Skattebo was heated for the flag.

“[Skattebo] was pissed off when he got the personal foul,” he said. “It’s football. Play football. We’re not playing patty-cake.”

Despite the fine, officials typically do not call penalties for illegal use of the helmet, which prompted Skattebo’s response.

The seven other players who got fined but not flagged were: Steelers receiver Brandon Smith ($4,916); 49ers running back Jordan James ($6,194); Colts cornerback Cam Taylor-Britt ($7,791); Bears cornerback Clark Phillips ($11,550); Broncos safety Brandon Jones ($23,882); Lions safety Brian Branch ($23,882); and Broncos Alex Singleton ($47,662).

Each week, the California Post will power rank the NBA’s 30 teams. Records are as of Saturday morning:

The Rockets take the top spot despite suffering their first loss of the season Friday to the Mavericks. Statistically, they have the league’s best offense and are getting contributions from across the board. Seven Rockets are averaging double-digit scoring figures. (Last week, 5th)

The league’s last undefeated team continues to climb up the rankings after another perfect week. The Grizzlies were the fun preseason pick when asked which team would exceed expectations. And with Ty Jerome and Cameron Boozer leading the way, they’ve done that so far. (Last week, 13th)

Two wins in 10 days over the defending NBA champions? It’s fair to say LeBron James, Tyrese Maxey, Jaylen Brown and Joel Embiid are headed in the right direction and could lead the 76ers to being legitimate NBA title contenders. (Last week, 2nd)

The Pistons have hardly missed a beat since All-NBA center Jalen Duren suffered a right hamstring strain that’ll sideline him for at least another week. Superstar guard Cade Cunningham leads a Pistons roster that’s getting contributions from all over as they look to build off a 60-win season last year. (Last week, 9th)

The Celtics have bounced back after dropping their season opener to the Pistons, rattling off four straight wins. Paul George has been a great fit, and Jayson Tatum is getting back to looking like his pre-Achilles injury self. (Last week, 10th)

The week went from bad to worse for the 2025 NBA champions. Three starters (Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren and Cason Wallace) suffered injuries that’ll sideline them for various periods. And the Thunder lost their first game after opening the season with four straight victories. (Last week, 1st)

The Spurs have bounced back from a slow start to the season with three straight wins. Victor Wembanyama is back to playing like the two-way force the Spurs need him to be to build off their 2026 NBA Finals appearance. (Last week, 4th)

The Trail Blazers started off hot, winning their first three games of the season before losing to the Grizzlies. But now, they face an uncertain immediate future with Ja Morant sidelined for at least the next month because of a strained left hamstring. (Last week, 12th)

The Lakers enter the weekend with the taste of their blown 25-point lead during the loss to the Warriors still fresh in their mouths. Luka Doncic (league-leading 36.2 points per game) is having an MVP-caliber start to the season, but this past week exposed some flaws. (Last week, 6th)

The Timberwolves were as hot as any team to start the season, but Anthony Edwards having a procedure on his right knee that could sideline him for a couple of months cooled them off. (Last week, 7th)

The Mavericks rattled off three straight wins this past week, and 2025-26 Rookie of the Year Cooper Flagg is looking like he’s taken a leap. Flagg is averaging 26.8 points, 6.6 assists, 6 rebounds, 2.6 steals and 1.2 blocked shots. (Last week, 15th)

The Raptors only got two games from Kawhi Leonard before swelling in his left knee sidelined the star forward. Scottie Barnes is poised to lead the Raptors while Leonard is out. (Last week, 8th)

The Cavaliers’ losses came against teams expected to be in the playoff race. They’re performing at their expected level but need more from James Harden to be a true contender in the East. (Last week, 14th)

Three straight wins over potential playoff teams, including the epic comeback against the Lakers, have the Warriors climbing back up the rankings after a slow start. Steph Curry’s third in the league in scoring (29.2 points). (Last week, 26th)

You can only play the teams in front of you, but the Nuggets’ victories have come against the lowly Pelicans and a Suns team that came out of the gates slowly. They need Nikola Jokic to get back to his MVP form. (Last week, 11th)

Nickeil Alexander-Walker is proving that last season’s breakout year wasn’t a fluke as the Hawks ended the week with a victory over the Cavaliers. (Last week, 18th)

The defending champions haven’t looked like it, with an 0-3 start turning into a disappointing October. There will be several opportunities to get back on track and stack wins throughout November. (Last week, 3rd)

Anthony Davis (22.3 points, 9.2 rebounds) and Trae Young (20.7 points, 10.2 assists) have led the Wizards to a respectable record and standing throughout the league so far. (Last week, 23rd)

It may not be the most efficient brand of basketball, but Brandon Miller is keeping the Hornets afloat as they wait for Coby White and Kon Knueppel to make their season debuts. (Last week, 19th)

Giannis Antetokounmpo continued to stuff the stat sheet (28.2 points, 12.3 rebounds, 5.5 assists), and the Heat finally picked up their first wins of the season against the Hawks and Pacers to close out the week ahead of an early West Coast swing. (Last week, 17th)

Road wins over the Knicks and Raptors this past week put the Magic in as good of a spot as possible despite an early-season ankle injury for Paolo Banchero. (Last week, 20th)

Tyrese Haliburton’s hamstring injury, which is expected to sideline him for two weeks, took the energy out of the start of the season. The Pacers entered the weekend having lost their previous three games. (Last week, 16th)

The Suns went from a gritty, tough style of play last season to having the league’s worst defense this year. They have to address the less glamorous end of the floor to get back on track. (Last week, 22nd)

The injuries continue to stack up for the Clippers, who signed Blake Wesley on a 10-day hardship deal in light of who they don’t have available. (Last week, 25th)

The Pelicans picked up their first win with their victory over the Kings on Thursday, but they still remain without a clear direction. (Last week, 27th)

Injuries that’ve zapped their frontcourt depth (Jaren Jackson Jr., Jusuf Nurkić) have slowed down what could’ve been a promising start to the season. (Last week, 21st)

Prioritizing the development of young players typically comes at a cost, even when it’s the right direction for a franchise. The Bulls continue to learn this lesson. (Last week, 24th)

The Bucks are feeling the growing pains after trading Antetokounmpo. (Last week, 30th)

At least the Nets have been competitive in a couple of their games so far. (Last week, 29th)

Meanwhile, the Kings are getting blown out regularly. (Last week, 28th)

news.originalContent:
The two individuals have been isolated while officials carry out contact tracing and laboratory testing.

Nigeria has identified two suspected Ebola cases in the northeast, after the country declared its first case in more than a decade on October 20.

Nigerian health authorities are investigating, and the two individuals have been isolated while contact tracing and laboratory testing get under way.

“Two suspected cases of Ebola disease have been identified in Nigeria’s northeast region,” the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention said in a statement posted on X on Saturday.

“Both individuals have been isolated, contact identification and listing is ongoing, and laboratory testing is being conducted.

“Being classified as suspected cases does not mean they are confirmed Ebola cases; confirmation is subject to laboratory results,” it added.

Last week, Nigeria became the fifth country to be affected by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola after an imported case was reported.

A Swiss woman who had travelled to Nigeria from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She and her husband, a Swiss diplomat, were evacuated to Switzerland on Monday.

The current outbreak emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in May.

The Bundibugyo strain has killed more than 5,000 people in the DRC since then.

The outbreak is the largest in the DRC’s history, affecting eight of the country’s 26 provinces and with more than 10,300 confirmed cases reported.

There is currently no approved treatment or vaccine for this strain of Ebola, but vaccine trials are under way.

The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) on Friday called for stronger measures to protect front-line workers after two young Congolese doctors died from Ebola earlier this week in DRC’s North Kivu and Ituri provinces.

Persistent weaknesses in early detection and contact tracing are among the main obstacles to stopping the current Ebola transmission in the DRC, according to health authorities.

Only about 12 percent of confirmed cases in the DRC have been identified among previously known contacts, with many deaths occurring in communities, authorities said.

Since May, Bundibugyo cases have been reported in the DRC, Uganda, France, Kenya and most recently, Nigeria.

news.originalContent:
The monument has sparked fierce opposition from local governments fearing disruption to traffic and historic views.

The District of Columbia (DC) and the state of Virginia have filed a joint lawsuit to halt the construction of a large triumphal arch sought by United States President Donald Trump.

Filed on Saturday, the lawsuit denounces the project as “flagrantly unlawful” and “legally indefensible”.

It calls on the federal court system to bar construction before it starts.

Otherwise, the lawsuit warns, Trump could claim that pausing construction already under way would pose a national security risk, as he has done with other controversial projects in the past.

“This is not the first time that Defendants have rushed to dramatically remake the District too quickly for courts to intervene,” the lawsuit reads. “This Court should not allow this effort to escape judicial scrutiny.”

Saturday’s complaint brings the total number of lawsuits against the arch to three.

Trump has championed the prospect of building a triumphal arch, similar to the Arc de Triomphe built in Paris during Napoleonic times.

Trump’s arch, however, is designed to stand 30 metres (100 feet) taller than the Statue of Liberty. It would tower from the Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, at 76 metres (250ft).

That colossal scale has prompted outrage, particularly from veterans’ groups who fear the arch would block views of Arlington National Cemetery, a hallowed military grave site.

White House officials maintain that ground could be broken as early as next week, on or around November 5.

On Friday, the administration unveiled a 106-page proposal for the arch to be a 12-storey megastructure, featuring a winged bronze statue of Lady Liberty lifting an eternal flame.

The arch would include two mezzanines and an observation deck with panoramic east-west views, as well as programme spaces, offices and a “fire command centre”.

Trump has previously said the arch would double as a military hub with snipers and drone capabilities.

Construction on the arch would also result in significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic to nearby roads.

news.originalContent:

The president and CEO of the American Psychological Association rejected the findings of a House report on Jew-hatred in the association, telling colleagues on Thursday that the APA has “held listening sessions” with Jewish psychologists.

“The APA’s actions not only create a harmful environment for Jewish members but also raise broader concerns about the profession,” a House Committee on Education and Workforce spokesperson told JNS.

“When an organization responsible for accrediting psychology programs and shaping professional standards allows ideology to overshadow scholarship, it risks undermining the credibility of the entire field,” the spokesperson said.

The report, released on Thursday, found that anti-Israel and anti-Jewish activists had “successfully co-opted” the association.

Internal emails showed that association leaders removed references to terrorism from their Oct. 7 statement following objections from an affiliated group.

The report also documented opposition to recognizing a Jewish ethnic psychological association, with critics arguing that Jews benefited from “white privilege.”

“The committee will not only continue to stand up for Jewish psychologists but will work to expose antisemitism wherever it occurs,” the committee spokesperson told JNS.

Following the report’s release, APA president Wendi S. Williams and CEO Arthur C. Evans, Jr., sent an email to colleagues, which JNS has viewed.

“We don’t agree with this report, they wrote. “The American Psychological Association unequivocally condemns antisemitism in all its forms.”

Stay up on the very latest with Evening Update.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

The association said it has “held listening sessions with more than 120 Jewish psychologists and stakeholders to better understand concerns” and “established a Collaborative of Jewish Psychologists to support continued engagement.”

“We recognize that this work requires continued attention and action, and we remain committed to advancing APA’s mission to promote well-being and respect for all,” Williams and Evans wrote.

The Anti-Defamation League issued a public statement on Friday, sent to JNS, thanking the House committee for the report.

“Antisemitism at the American Psychological Association is not isolated,” the organization stated. “It is embedded in its ranks and in its leadership.”

The ADL stated that it and other Jewish organizations “publicly and privately told APA leadership exactly what needed to change, and it failed to act” for more than a year.

“When a healing profession treats one group’s pain with such indifference, Jewish patients are right to wonder whether they will be met with compassion or with contempt,” ADL stated.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A witness to the deadly shooting inside a Halloween store at a Bay Area mall described the terrifying scene as shots rang out and she ducked for cover — fearing she was “going to die” as several victims were struck by gunfire.

Jocelyn Lopez Tabares, 15, and her 23-year-old sister were picking up last-minute accessories for their costumes Friday night at the Spirit Halloween store at the Solano Town Center in Fairfield when a barrage of shots erupted.

“I felt like I was going to die,” Lopez Tabares, of Vallejo, told the California Post. “I thought it was going to be my last time living. I didn’t want to die that way.”

The shooting, which left one person dead and six others injured, was a “targeted incident” carried out by a lone gunman, police announced. The suspect remained on the run as of Saturday afternoon. Lopez Tabares, who was standing near the checkout registers, initially mistook the gunfire for popping balloons, until her sister dragged her to the concrete floor, she recalled.

“We were in line getting ready to leave,” Lopez Tabares said. “Out of nowhere, we just hear at least 10 shots go off. I thought it was a balloon popping. I was in shock, and everyone just went down. My sister pulled me down because I couldn’t move. I was so scared.”

As dozens of shoppers scrambled toward the exits in panic, the 15-year-old found herself frozen on the floor.

“All I could hear was people screaming and running from the back to the front,” she said.

The teen then pulled out her cellphone and began recording, determined to document the scene in case she did not survive.

“I just had a feeling to do it… to record for evidence,” she said. “And then after I stopped the video, I called my mom, because what if I wasn’t going to make it out of there?”

The footage shows the panic inside the store as people drop between merchandise racks and frantically take cover. Lopez Tabares said she later shared the clip online after seeing early social media rumors questioning whether a shooting had even happened.

Within minutes of the rapid gunfire, the bustling shop was nearly deserted, leaving only the sisters and a handful of terrified patrons hiding on the floor.

That was when she heard the desperate cries of a frantic mother echoing through the aisles.

“All I could hear was this mom yelling, ‘My baby, he’s dead!’ She was just crying for him,” Lopez Tabares recalled. “She was like, ‘My son… you guys can’t leave him here.’ She looked at my sister, but we couldn’t do anything.”

Authorities have not identified the person who was killed.

Other shoppers inside the retailer described a similarly surreal scene.

Witness Miena Davis told KCRA that shoppers initially froze after hearing popping sounds before a second round of gunfire sent people stampeding toward the mall entrance.

“It was immediate panic,” Davis said. “You heard a mom crying out for their child. And it just was so surreal.”

When Lopez Tabares and her sister finally stood up to run for their lives, they encountered a horrific scene near the exit.

“While we were walking out, there were bodies right there,” she told The Post. “There were two bodies… they were not moving at all.”

Shaken and terrified, the sisters reached their car and drove to their Vallejo home.

The shooting occurred around 8:30 p.m. inside the pop-up retailer at the former Best Buy space.

Fairfield police announced Saturday morning that detectives are investigating the attack as a “targeted incident” carried out by a lone gunman who fled the property before officers arrived.

The FBI’s Sacramento Evidence Response Team has joined local detectives to investigate.

news.originalContent:

Americans are getting the majority of their news from social media, according to a new report.

Syracuse University’s Center for the Creator Economy found in its latest monthly Flash Report that social media platforms have overtaken traditional TV news as the most frequently cited source of political and election news among adults surveyed.

The survey of 1,001 adults found that 59% regularly get their news from social media, while 55% turn to those platforms for political information.

Young adults and black Americans were among the groups most likely to rely on social media for news, rather than professional journalists.

Taken together, social platforms and independent outlets — including YouTube, X, TikTok, Instagram, podcasts, Substack and independent newsletters — were cited by 60% of respondents, compared with 32% who cited traditional newsrooms, according to the report.

Leading the pack — YouTube.

The video giant ranks as America’s top individual source for political and election news, capturing 16.5% of readers, narrowly beating broadcast and cable TV news at 16.1% and online news sites at 15.7%.

X registered 14%, Facebook followed with 10.8%, TikTok with 10.4%, Instagram at 7.3%, podcasts at 3.5%, Substack or newsletters at 3.4% and LinkedIn coming in last at a lackluster 0.3%.

The findings also suggest that audiences increasingly judge news by who delivers it, rather than by traditional credentials.

A whopping 61% of Americans reported they trust a well-known independent news creator as much as a well-known professional journalist or a major news organization on political topics. And 67% said who does the reporting matters more than formal journalism credentials.

When it comes to correcting mistakes, 86% said public corrections by independent news creators increase their trust in those creators — the strongest trust-related finding cited in the study.

But traditional journalists haven’t lost all credibility: 79% of respondents still recognized a meaningful difference between independent news creators and professional journalists.

Politics also plays a major role in whom audiences trust.

Republicans generally show greater trust in independent news creators while Democrats lean toward established journalists and news organizations, the report said.

The doctor who oversaw Christa Pike’s botched execution compared himself to Jesus, still wants her put to death,  and said in his first public comments since the fiasco that he’s willing to finish the job himself.

Dr. Mark Fowler, a 69-year-old grandfather and Bible school teacher studying at seminary, said he believes Pike deserves to die for the brutal 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, he told New York Magazine.

For two reasons. One, because it would bring “a sense of justice” to her victim’s mother, who was present at the execution attempt.

And two, because he there’s “no doubt” in his mind that the inmates he has personally helped put to death deserved their punishment.

“There are times when you have to draw a line and say, ‘You have traversed socially acceptable norms and we must extract from you the ultimate penalty,” Fowler told the news outlet.

Fowler, whose role during Pike’s execution was to wait in a death chamber anteroom and then pronounce her dead, has taken part in seven executions at $3,000 a job — and believes carrying out the death sentence is a moral obligation.

“How can you morally say, ‘I’m for the death penalty so long as someone else does the work?'” he said. “I do things that nobody wants to do.”

On Sept. 30, Fowler was waiting when prison officials called him into the death chamber where Pike was still breathing after two doses of the lethal drug phenobarbital.

He said he knew something was wrong because it had been 45 minutes since the start of the procedure, which usually takes about 10 minutes.

“She’s not dead,” the warden told him.

Fowler thought it was just a matter of time until she succumbed to the drug. He gave it another half hour.

But at that point, Pike, 50, remained comatose, the deputy commissioner ordered the execution to stop, and Fowler was forced to arrange emergency treatment to save her life.

Investigators later determined that Pike’s IV lines had been improperly placed and caused the drugs to seep into the tissue in her arms instead of entering her bloodstream.

In less than two weeks, she was walking and talking and back in prison at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Nashville, Tennessee.

The state’s governor, Bill Lee, suspended executions for the rest of 2026, while Pike’s lawyers try to prevent another lethal injection.

Fowler admitted mistakes were made, saying staff should have responded when Pike complained of arm pain.

“They should have stopped and reassessed, and they didn’t,” he said.

Now he wants Tennessee to consider returning to a three-drug execution cocktail that includes potassium chloride, despite concerns that it’s a painful way to go.

But Fowler doesn’t see himself as a bad guy.

“I’m not an evil, vicious person. I’m not unscrupulous. I’m not uncaring, and I’m not incompetent,” he insisted.

California’s likely next governor is still struggling to say exactly what he’d do about the state’s biggest problems — and a head-scratching answer about the housing crisis is drawing fresh ridicule just before Election Day.

Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra went viral after a recent interview with the San Francisco Chronicle in which reporters pressed him to take a position on one of California’s most contentious housing debates.

The question: Is he a YIMBY or a NIMBY?

Instead of picking a side, Becerra offered a philosophical detour.

“It’s interesting, YIMBY-NIMBY.”

“There’s some people who don’t have a backyard at all, and who never get to engage in that YIMBY-NIMBY debate,” the Democrat added.

The exchange prompted one Chronicle editor to say journalists “tried to get him to say literally anything substantive.”

The terms refer to opposing sides of California’s housing fight. NIMBYs, or “Not In My Backyard” advocates, resist new housing developments in their neighborhoods, while YIMBYs, or “Yes In My Backyard” supporters, push for more construction to address the state’s housing shortage.

Becerra’s answer left plenty of Californians wondering where he actually stands.

Housing advocate Toby Muresianu joked: “Finally, a politician with the courage to say ‘Maybe in my backyard?’ What is a backyard anyway, really?”

Former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt was less amused.

LMAO Xavier Basura may be the most pathetic NPC candidate I've ever seen. Zero charisma, zero clue, zero campaigning…it's such a slap in the face of CA democrats to run this guy. Almost as if they're pranking them to see how much insanity they'll accept for tribalism. https://t.co/TWZlQegIAJ

“Zero charisma, zero clue, zero campaigning,” Pratt said. “It’s such a slap in the face of CA democrats to run this guy. Almost as if they’re pranking them to see how much insanity they’ll accept for tribalism.”

Others questioned whether Becerra understood the backyard reference was metaphorical, while some tried to decipher whether his answer signaled support for more development or opposition to it.

His campaign website promises an executive order declaring a housing shortage state of emergency and directing state agencies to make housing production a top priority. But he also pledges to “keep communities intact as we build.”

That balancing act has become a recurring feature of Becerra’s campaign.

In August, he told CalMatters that his reluctance to offer detailed policy promises stemmed from a political lesson he learned more than three decades ago.

As a freshman congressman representing the Los Angeles area in 1993, Becerra initially opposed the North American Free Trade Agreement before eventually voting for it after being persuaded that labor protections and a domestic lending program would protect American workers.

He later said those assurances failed to prevent American jobs from being displaced.

“No one gets my vote unless I know what I’m voting for completely,” he told the outlet, describing the experience as a “pivotal lesson.”

Now, Becerra says he doesn’t want to make promises he can’t keep — including putting a number on how many homes he would build as governor.

“I would prefer not to run on inflated promises,” he once said. “I will run on my record.”

But with California voters still grappling with a housing affordability crisis, his reluctance to spell out specifics is giving critics plenty of ammunition.

And Becerra may have little political incentive to change course. Recent polling shows him building a double-digit lead over Republican challenger Steve Hilton in a state where Democrats vastly outnumber Republicans.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman insisted Saturday that recent polls showing Gov. Kathy Hochul widening her lead heading into Election Day are “inaccurate,” claiming the race is a “virtual dead heat.”

“Don’t believe those phony polls,” the Nassau County executive told more than 100 supporters at a campaign rally at Juniper Valley Park in Middle Village, Queens.

He was referring to polls released Wednesday by Siena and Marist showing Hochul leading the race by 14 points and 11 points, respectively.

Blakeman also claimed he’ll pull off an upset like former Republican Gov. George Pataki did in 1994, saying polls were “wrong” then as well.

Among those in attendance were Queens GOP Chairman Tony Nunziato, Councilwoman Joann Ariola (R-Queens) and ex-Councilman Robert Holden (D-Queens).

The Nassau County executive was also expected to ramp up his get-out-the-vote efforts later in the day by hitting Halloween parades in Maspeth and Glendale and meeting with voters throughout the Upper East Side, while Hochul was scheduled to make campaign stops in Huntington and Brookhaven on Long Island, and in Brooklyn and Queens.

The campaigns traded Halloween-themed attacks Saturday as they made their final pitches to voters.

Blakeman’s social media accounts posted AI-generated photos and video of Hochul dressed as a witch.

“Forget witches. The real Halloween nightmare is four more years of Kathy Hochul!” Blakeman said on X. “DITCH THE WITCH!”

Hochul’s camp sent out a mass email ripping Blakeman’s armed, civilian-volunteer “emergency special deputy sheriffs” program — labeling it as a “militia clusterf**k.”
